subtype: Approach: building a support network early [Thinking]
passage: The new tenant in 4B, Pooja, did not look like someone in a hurry to be lonely. In her first month I saw her come home with a small clay pot from a pottery class, and leave on Saturday for the hobby group at the community hall. An old college friend, Uday, came for tea one Sunday, and the two of them spent half the afternoon laughing on the balcony. Pooja asked me where a trusted doctor was and which grocery shop delivered; I sent her to the clinic on the corner and the shop by the temple. I don't know what she felt walking into a room of strangers. Some evenings she came home quiet. But every week another new name slipped into her stories about the day.

qa.q: Which two places did the narrator recommend to Pooja?
qa.a: The clinic on the corner and the grocery shop by the temple.

qa.q: What might Pooja have felt walking into a room of strangers, according to the narrator?
qa.a: The narrator does not know for sure, but Pooja may have felt nervous or a little lonely, since some evenings she came home quiet.

qa.q: What could Pooja do if loneliness returns?
qa.a: She could keep seeing Uday, go to more group meetings and introduce herself to more neighbours.

qa.q: How does the narrator see Pooja's first month?
qa.a: The narrator sees Pooja as steadily building connections, while admitting not being able to know what she felt inside.

grounding: Pooja joins a hobby group, contacts an old college friend and finds a doctor and grocery shop in her first month.

subtype: Approach: building a support network early [Thinking]
passage:
Week one. Nirmala had moved to Pune for her new job and knew nobody. On Friday night she ate dinner standing at the kitchen counter and felt the silence of the flat press in. She'd read that loneliness hits many people who move. "I'm not waiting for it to hit me," she thought. She opened her phone and found a Sunday morning cycling group near her area.
Week two. She messaged Jyoti, an old college friend who lived across the city. "Coffee on Saturday?" They talked for three hours. Jyoti gave her the name of a doctor she trusted in Aundh, and a grocery shop that delivered.
Week four. Nirmala had cycled three Sundays, knew two people by name, and had a doctor's number saved. When she caught a cold, she didn't panic. She called the clinic and messaged Jyoti, who dropped off soup.

qa.q: Which day did the cycling group meet?
How did Nirmala feel on the first Friday night?
qa.a: Nirmala felt lonely, eating standing up while the silence of the flat pressed in.

qa.q: What else could Nirmala do to strengthen the support network?
qa.a: Nirmala could get to know a neighbour or a colleague outside work, so there are people nearby as well as across the city.

qa.q: How might Jyoti see Nirmala's message after so long?
qa.a: Jyoti seems happy to reconnect and glad to help, sharing a trusted doctor and later bringing soup.

grounding: It shows someone expecting loneliness after a move and, over the first month, joining a hobby group, contacting an old friend and finding a trusted doctor and grocery store.

subtype: Approach: building a support network early [Thinking]
passage:
Hansa, you've just moved to Delhi and you sound lonely on the phone. Let me, Zainab, your Phuppo, tell you what I did when I moved to Hyderabad for my first job in 1995.
Everyone warned me the first months in a new city are the loneliest. So I didn't wait for friends to find me.
In the very first week, I joined the evening Urdu poetry circle at the library near my hostel. I was terrible at reciting, but it gave me somewhere to be on Thursdays.
The same week, I wrote a letter to Shabnam, my college roommate, who lived in Secunderabad. She came on Sunday with biryani.
I asked the older women in the hostel which lady doctor they trusted, and which kirana shop gave fair weights. I had both names written in my diary by the end of the month.
When I got fever that winter, I wasn't alone. That's the whole secret, Hansa. Build the net before you fall.

qa.q: On which day did the poetry circle meet?
How did Zainab feel about the poetry circle despite being bad at reciting?
qa.a: Zainab felt it was worth it, glad to have somewhere to belong on Thursdays even though reciting was hard.

qa.q: What was the key choice in Zainab's story, and why did it matter later?
qa.a: The key choice was building a network in the first month; it mattered because when fever came that winter, Zainab had friends, a trusted doctor and a shop to rely on.

qa.q: How might Shabnam have felt receiving Zainab's letter?
qa.a: Shabnam was probably happy and eager to reconnect, coming that Sunday with biryani.

grounding: It shows an elder recalling how, expecting loneliness after a move, she joined a group, contacted an old friend and found a trusted doctor and grocery store in the first month.
